title: Throw away your bow
hookLine: on the mountain, a glowing ascetic tells Arjuna to throw away his bow, and Arjuna keeps to his own path
carry: svadharma: walk your own path, not another's
tomorrow: why would a warrior live on air?

lines: WHAT ARE YOU DOING WITH THOSE?
cards: Stop. The word rings out across a mountain slope in the north, and Arjuna stops. He has walked a long way, bow in hand, quiver on his back, toward a peak the epic calls Indrakila.

Under a tree sits an ascetic: thin, matted hair, glowing with the strength of long discipline. He looks at the armed young man and asks, more or less: what are you doing with those? This is a place of peace.
The first test of Arjuna's austerities doesn't look like a test at all.

teach.b: The ascetic goes on. Here, he says, live peaceful seekers who have left anger behind. There's no need for weapons in this place.
Throw away your bow. You've already reached a high state. He asks again and again.
But Arjuna won't put the bow down. He won't leave his brothers waiting in the forest, he says, and go off to some peaceful world without the weapons he came for.
Then the ascetic shows who he really is: Indra, king of the gods, and in the story Arjuna's own father. Pleased, he offers his son a boon. Arjuna asks for weapons.
Indra answers: first, you must see Shiva, the three-eyed god who holds the trident. Then I'll give you mine. So the first test isn't whether he can give everything up.
It's whether he'll stay on his own path when a holy one offers another. And the epic plants a seed here.

Years later, at Kurukshetra, Arjuna himself will drop his bow and want to walk away, and Krishna will answer him in the Bhagavad Gita: better your own dharma, even done imperfectly, than another's done well.
That's svadharma: your own duty, fitted to who you are and where you stand. A hermit's peace is holy, and for the hermit it is dharma. But Arjuna has brothers waiting and a promise to keep.
For him, laying the bow down here would mean walking someone else's path. The Gita's question isn't whose path is holier. It's whether you're on yours.

how: Retellings of the Mahabharata follow Arjuna to the mountain, where Indra tests him in disguise before sending him to seek Shiva; Hindu teachers link the scene to svadharma, one's own duty, which Krishna teaches Arjuna in the Bhagavad Gita.

Hindu teaching says everyone must leave the world to be truly spiritual
svadharma: the hermit's way is holy for the hermit; a warrior's duty is his own.

games.q: a friend says real spirituality means dropping your commitments and going off to meditate. by Arjuna's test, what's closer to Hindu teaching?
o: it depends on your svadharma: the hermit's peace is his path, not everyone's.
yes: everyone should leave their duties for the forest.
no: meditation has no place in Hindu life.
games.why: Indra was pleased that Arjuna kept his bow. the Gita says it later: better your own dharma, imperfect, than another's done well.

practice: Sit still and bring to mind the roles you hold right now: child, friend, student, worker, parent. Breathe in and name one; breathe out and ask, what is my dharma in this one, today?
If someone else's path keeps calling, let it pass like weather on a mountain. If you pray, ask to know your own dharma; if not, just name it.

wordCard.voice: Arjuna's austerities. They begin on a mountain, where an ascetic tells him to throw away his bow, and Arjuna keeps to his own path.

orig.note: Sanskrit svadharma: one's own dharma, the duty fitted to who you are.

carryVoice: Your line: svadharma: walk your own path, not another's. Arjuna's first test was a holy-sounding invitation to leave his. Tomorrow: why would a warrior live on air? That's day seven hundred eighty-two.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Aranyaka Parva), Kairata Parva opening (Arjuna reaches Indrakila; Indra appears as an ascetic, tests him, reveals himself and sends him to seek Shiva)
Bhagavad Gita 3.35 (better one's own dharma, though imperfect, than another's well performed; echoed at 18.47)
